newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges restraint at Israel-Lebanon border.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges restraint at Israel-Lebanon border.

text.p: The United States on Friday condemned renewed cross border attacks between Israel and Lebanon and urged all sides to exercise "maximum restraint" in ending the violence.

With the tense border situation compounding a crisis between Israel and the Palestinians, State Department spokesman James Rubin expressed concern that the attacks could lead to an escalation of violence in the region.
He said Washington had told Israel, Lebanon, Syria and the pro-Iranian Hizbollah rebel group via Lebanon that "this is no time for escalation, this is no time to see civilians suffer."
"We've been in contact with all the parties directly to urge maximum restraint ... We want that to stop," he told a news briefing.

Rockets fired from Lebanon slammed into a town in northern Israel on Friday, escalating violence that has killed 13 people this week, and Israeli warplanes retaliated by rocketing guerrilla targets south of Beirut.
Rubin said the Katuysha rockets fired into Israel clearly violated a 1996 U.S.-brokered agreement establishing a ceasefire at the border.
As for whether the Israel retaliation also violated the accord, he said that depended on what the Israeli targets were. The accord bans attacks on civilians.
A monitoring group that includes Israel, the United States, France, Syria and Lebanon plans to meet this weekened to investiogate the attacks.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross was due to leave Washignton on Friday night on a weekend mission to the region to mediate between Israel and the Palestinians.
He is due to lay ground for Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's first Middle East visit later in August.
Albright, in a major speech this week, said Ross would focus on security issues and she would need to see "some progress" in that regard for her trip to go forward.
But Rubin over the past two days has made clear U.S. standards are so minimal in this regard there is little chance she would not go.
"If we had 100 percent effort (from the Palestinians in cracking down on terrorism), she will go. And by the way, she would also go if there were some progress," he said.
Rubin, at Friday's briefing, complained that since Albright's speech "we have not seen the kind of security cooperation from the Palestinians that we would have hoped."
"And as you know, we weren't thrilled with some of the rhetoric that was used by the Israeli side, either," he said.

"So in that sense, we're not regarding the reaction as necessarily a good thing. But the speech isn't about what the reaction is in a day or two days ... (It) is about laying out America's role in the Middle East ... the test of whether the reaction to the speech will be good will come over time, not in a matter of a day or two," he said.
